posts.post_title: Who is regarded as the father of chemotherap…
posts.post_content: Who is regarded as the father of chemotherapy?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Paul Ehrlich

Paul Ehrlich is called the father of chemotherapy.

Correct Option Explanation

Ehrlich proposed that dyes selectively staining microbes could also be selectively toxic to them, and developed arsenicals such as arsphenamine (1909) for syphilis, coining the term chemotherapy.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928 from a contaminated Penicillium culture plate.
  • Gerhard Domagk demonstrated the therapeutic effect of Prontosil in 1935, ushering in the modern era of chemotherapy.
  • Selman Waksman discovered streptomycin in 1944 after a systematic search of Actinomycetes.
Know More
  • Ehrlich developed atoxyl for sleeping sickness before arsphenamine.
  • The term chemotherapy was coined because Ehrlich used drugs of known chemical structure.
  • Domagk, Fleming-Chain-Florey and Waksman all received the Nobel Prize for their discoveries.
  • The empirical phase of chemotherapy included use of cinchona bark for fevers and mercury for syphilis by Paracelsus.

posts.post_title: Prontosil was demonstrated effective in whic…
posts.post_content: In which year did Domagk demonstrate the therapeutic effect of Prontosil, a sulfonamide dye, in pyogenic infection?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 1935

Domagk demonstrated Prontosil's effect in 1935, ushering in the modern era of chemotherapy.

Correct Option Explanation

Prontosil was later found to work through its active moiety, para-amino benzene sulfonamide, not the dye portion itself.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 1929 is the year Fleming discovered penicillin in England, not when Prontosil was demonstrated.
  • 1932 is close to when Prontosil (a sulphonamide) was discovered in Germany but predates Domagk's therapeutic demonstration.
  • 1941 marks the year penicillin entered clinical use following Chain and Florey's work.
Know More
  • Sulfapyridine (M&B 693) was the first sulfonamide marketed, in 1938.
  • Penicillin was purified for clinical use by Chain and Florey in 1939, culminating in clinical use in 1941.
  • Domagk received the Nobel Prize in 1939 for this discovery.
  • The phenomenon of antibiosis was first demonstrated by Pasteur in 1877.

posts.post_title: Term for treatment of infections without har…
posts.post_content: The treatment of systemic infections with drugs that selectively suppress the infecting microorganism without significantly affecting the host is generally called what?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Chemotherapy

This selective treatment of infections is called chemotherapy.

Correct Option Explanation

Drugs in this class are designed to inhibit or kill the infecting organism while having minimal effect on the host, unlike drugs used for other conditions.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Chemoprophylaxis refers to preventive drug use, not the general term for selective treatment of established infection.
  • Antisepsis refers to prevention of infection on living tissue by inhibiting or destroying organisms, distinct from systemic chemotherapy.
  • Immunotherapy works through modulating the host immune system rather than directly suppressing the microorganism.
Know More
  • Due to analogy between malignant cells and pathogenic microbes, treatment of neoplastic disease with drugs is also called chemotherapy.
  • Antimicrobial agent (AMA) is the preferred term covering both synthetic and naturally obtained drugs.
  • Antimicrobial drugs are considered the greatest contribution of the last century to therapeutics.
  • Antibiotics are natural substances produced by microorganisms that suppress or kill other microorganisms at very low concentrations.

posts.post_title: Year streptomycin was discovered by Waksman
posts.post_content: In which year did Waksman and colleagues discover streptomycin during their systematic search of Actinomycetes?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 1944

Streptomycin was discovered in 1944 by Waksman's group.

Correct Option Explanation

This group of soil microbes (Actinomycetes) proved to be a treasure-house of antibiotics, subsequently yielding tetracyclines, chloramphenicol and erythromycin.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 1935 is the year Domagk demonstrated Prontosil's effect, not streptomycin's discovery.
  • 1938 is when the first sulfonamide (sulfapyridine, M&B 693) was marketed.
  • 1950 falls after streptomycin's discovery and after several other antibiotics like chloramphenicol (1947) had already been found.
Know More
  • Streptomycin was notably important for its activity against tubercle bacilli.
  • Waksman received the Nobel Prize for this discovery.
  • Nalidixic acid, the first quinolone, was introduced later in 1967.
  • The first cephalosporin became available for clinical use in 1964.

posts.post_content: Which class of antibacterial agents was the first entirely man-made, fully synthetic group, developed by structural modification of chloroquine?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Quinolones

Quinolones were the first entirely synthetic antibacterial agents.

Correct Option Explanation

They were developed from structural modification of chloroquine (1939), with nalidixic acid introduced in 1967 as the first quinolone.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Sulfonamides were synthesized from sulfanilamide but are generally classed as antibacterials, not the 'first entirely synthetic' historic landmark referenced here.
  • Aminoglycosides such as streptomycin are natural or semisynthetic products of Streptomyces species.
  • Tetracyclines include naturally occurring compounds like oxytetracycline derived from Streptomyces.
Know More
  • Fluorination at the 6th position and addition of a piperazine moiety in the 1980s led to fluoroquinolones.
  • First-generation quinolones include nalidixic acid, oxolinic acid and flumequine.
  • Second-generation quinolones include ciprofloxacin, danofloxacin, enrofloxacin and norfloxacin.
  • Fluoroquinolones act by inhibiting DNA gyrase.

posts.post_title: Type of resistance seen in gram negative vs…
posts.post_content: The natural insensitivity of gram-negative organisms to penicillin, due to lack of the required metabolic process or target sites, is an example of which type of resistance?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Natural resistance

This inherent, group-specific insensitivity is natural resistance.

Correct Option Explanation

Natural resistance occurs because some microbes always lack the metabolic process or target site for a drug; it is generally group specific and does not produce clinical problems.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Acquired resistance develops in an organism that was previously sensitive, due to AMA exposure over time, and poses a clinical problem.
  • Cross resistance refers to resistance to one drug conferring resistance to related drugs, not an organism's inherent insensitivity.
  • Infectious resistance is another name for gene-transfer-mediated acquired resistance, not natural resistance.
Know More
  • M. tuberculosis is naturally insensitive to tetracyclines.
  • Staphylococci, coliforms and tubercle bacilli are examples of bacteria that acquire rapid resistance.
  • Acquired resistance arises through mutation or gene transfer (infectious resistance).
  • Gene transfer can occur via conjugation, transduction, or transformation.

posts.post_title: Gene transfer through sex pilus formation
posts.post_content: Which mechanism of gene transfer involves sexual contact between bacteria through the formation of a bridge or sex pilus, common among gram-negative bacilli?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Conjugation

Sex-pilus-mediated gene transfer is called conjugation.

Correct Option Explanation

It frequently occurs in the colon, where a large variety of gram-negative bacilli come into close contact, and may involve the resistance transfer factor (RTF).

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Transduction transfers resistance genes via a bacteriophage vector, not a sex pilus.
  • Transformation involves uptake of free resistance-carrying DNA released into the medium by a resistant bacterium.
  • Mutation is a spontaneous, random genetic change, not a form of gene transfer between organisms.
Know More
  • Even nonpathogenic organisms may transfer R factor to pathogenic organisms via conjugation.
  • Chloramphenicol resistance in typhoid bacilli with concomitant multi-drug resistance has occurred by conjugation.
  • In transduction, the R factor is taken up by a phage and delivered to another bacterium it infects.
  • Transformation is considered probably not clinically significant compared to conjugation.

posts.post_title: Single gene mutation conferring high resista…
posts.post_content: A single gene mutation that confers a high degree of resistance and emerges rapidly, as seen in Enterococci against streptomycin, is called what type of mutation?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Single step mutation

This rapid, single-gene resistance mechanism is called a single step mutation.

Correct Option Explanation

A single gene mutation can confer high-degree resistance that emerges rapidly, as exemplified by Enterococci becoming resistant to streptomycin.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Multistep mutation involves a number of gene modifications developing gradually, e.g., resistance to erythromycin and tetracyclines.
  • Plasmid mutation is not the correct term used in this classification; plasmid-mediated resistance is a form of gene transfer, not mutation type.
  • Chromosomal transformation conflates two distinct resistance mechanisms (chromosomal mutation and transformation) inaccurately.
Know More
  • Mutation is a stable, heritable genetic change occurring spontaneously and is not induced by the AMA itself.
  • Sensitive populations with few mutant cells get selectively preserved when sensitive cells are eliminated due to lack of competition.
  • Antitubercular drug use alone commonly leads to this mutation-driven resistance pattern.
  • Multistep mutation resistance, by contrast, develops more gradually over time.

posts.post_title: Two main mechanisms of antimicrobial resista…
posts.post_content: What are the two broad mechanisms by which bacteria develop resistance to antimicrobial agents?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Mutation and gene transfer

The two broad mechanisms of resistance are mutation and gene transfer.

Correct Option Explanation

Gene transfer (infectious resistance) occurs via conjugation, transduction, or transformation, while mutation is a spontaneous heritable change.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Conjugation and transduction are both subtypes of gene transfer, not the two overall mechanism categories.
  • Efflux and permeability are specific resistance strategies at the cellular level, not the two overarching categories described in this text.
  • Enzymatic degradation and target modification describe specific molecular strategies rather than the two broad mechanisms named in the classification.
Know More
  • Transformation is considered the least clinically significant mode of gene transfer.
  • Selection pressure from widespread AMA use allows resistant subpopulations to thrive over sensitive ones.
  • Conjugation is a particularly important mechanism because it can spread resistance to pathogenic organisms via food or water contamination.
  • Resistance once acquired becomes prevalent primarily due to selection pressure of the drug in use.

posts.post_title: Organism causing anthrax growth inhibition b…
posts.post_content: Who demonstrated the phenomenon of antibiosis in 1877 by showing that growth of anthrax bacilli in urine was inhibited by airborne bacteria?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Louis Pasteur

Louis Pasteur demonstrated antibiosis in 1877.

Correct Option Explanation

He showed that growth of anthrax bacilli in urine was inhibited by airborne bacteria, laying groundwork for the later discovery of antibiotics.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Alexander Fleming demonstrated antibiosis later, in 1929, observing Penicillium mould inhibiting Staphylococcus growth.
  • Paul Ehrlich is associated with the dye and organometallic phase of chemotherapy (1890-1935), not the 1877 antibiosis demonstration.
  • Selman Waksman discovered streptomycin in 1944 through systematic search of Actinomycetes, decades after Pasteur's work.
Know More
  • Fleming named the diffusible antistaphylococcal substance he found penicillin but could not purify it.
  • Chain and Florey followed up Fleming's observation in 1939, leading to clinical use of penicillin in 1941.
  • Commercial manufacture of penicillin was accelerated due to its potential in treating war wounds.
  • Waksman subsequently found Actinomycetes to be a rich source of many other antibiotics.

posts.post_content: Bacterial conjugation, an important mechanism of resistance gene transfer among gram-negative bacilli, most frequently occurs in which body site?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Colon

Conjugation frequently occurs in the colon.

Correct Option Explanation

The colon harbors a large variety of gram-negative bacilli in close contact, facilitating transfer of resistance transfer factor (RTF) even from nonpathogenic to pathogenic organisms.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • The lungs are not cited as the primary site for this gene-transfer mechanism.
  • The kidney is not described as a site of conjugation in this context.
  • The bloodstream is not the site emphasized for conjugation; the colon's dense bacterial population is what is highlighted.
Know More
  • Contamination of food or water can spread resistant organisms arising from colonic conjugation.
  • Multi-drug resistance (MDR) acquisition via conjugation has been documented for chloramphenicol resistance in typhoid bacilli.
  • Transduction, by contrast, involves bacteriophage-mediated gene transfer.
  • Transformation involves uptake of free DNA released by a resistant bacterium into the medium.

posts.post_content: Which group of antimicrobial agents is classified together based on their mechanism of inhibiting bacterial cell wall synthesis?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Penicillin, cephalosporin, cycloserine, vancomycin, bacitracin

Penicillin, cephalosporin, cycloserine, vancomycin, and bacitracin inhibit cell wall synthesis.

Correct Option Explanation

These agents act on different steps of bacterial cell wall (peptidoglycan) formation, making them bactericidal against actively dividing bacteria.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Aminoglycosides and tetracyclines are classified as protein synthesis inhibitors, not cell wall synthesis inhibitors.
  • Sulfonamides and trimethoprim interfere with intermediary (folate) metabolism, not cell wall synthesis.
  • Fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase, while rifampin interferes with DNA-dependent RNA polymerase function, not cell wall synthesis.
Know More
  • Polypeptides and polyenes act by causing leakage from the cell membrane.
  • Aminoglycosides cause misreading of mRNA code and affect permeability.
  • Idoxuridine, acyclovir and zidovudine interfere with DNA synthesis.
  • Rifampin and metronidazole interfere with DNA function.

posts.post_content: Which pair of drugs exemplifies narrow-spectrum antimicrobial agents active against either gram-positive or gram-negative organisms only?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Penicillin and streptomycin

Penicillin and streptomycin are classic examples of narrow-spectrum agents.

Correct Option Explanation

Narrow-spectrum agents act against either gram-positive (penicillin) or gram-negative (streptomycin) organisms, unlike broad-spectrum drugs active against both.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Tetracyclines and chloramphenicol are cited as broad-spectrum agents active against both gram-positive and gram-negative organisms.
  • Erythromycin has a spectrum similar to penicillin but wider, and doxycycline is a broad-spectrum tetracycline, so this pairing does not fit the narrow-spectrum example.
  • Ciprofloxacin and cefepime represent newer extended-spectrum agents, not the classic narrow-spectrum example cited in the text.
Know More
  • Erythromycin is also cited as an example of a broad-spectrum agent alongside tetracyclines and chloramphenicol.
  • Newer extended-spectrum penicillins, cephalosporins, and fluoroquinolones now offer broader coverage than earlier narrow-spectrum agents.
  • Some agents can additionally act on rickettsia and protozoa.
  • Antimicrobials are also classified by bactericidal versus bacteriostatic action.

posts.post_title: Which drugs are described as bactericidal ty…
posts.post_content: Which of the following groups are classified as bactericidal based on type of action?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Penicillins, aminoglycosides, polypeptides, vancomycin, ciprofloxacin

Penicillins, aminoglycosides, polypeptides, vancomycin and ciprofloxacin are bactericidal.

Correct Option Explanation

These agents actively kill bacteria rather than merely inhibiting their growth, which is the defining feature of bactericidal action.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Sulfonamides and tetracyclines are classified as bacteriostatic agents.
  • Chloramphenicol and erythromycin are also classified as bacteriostatic under type of action.
  • Trimethoprim alone is bacteriostatic; it only becomes bactericidal in combination with a sulfonamide.
Know More
  • Some static drugs, like nitrofurantoin and sulfa, may become cidal at high concentrations such as in the urinary tract.
  • Bacteriostatic drugs rely on the host's immune defense to eliminate the pathogen.
  • Antimicrobials are also classified by their source, such as fungi, bacteria, or Actinomycetes.
  • Fungi as a source yield penicillin, cephalosporins, and griseofulvin.

posts.post_content: Antibiotics such as aminoglycosides, tetracyclines, chloramphenicol, macrolides and polyenes are classified based on source as being derived from which group of organisms?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Actinomycetes

These antibiotic classes are derived from Actinomycetes.

Correct Option Explanation

Actinomycetes are a group of soil-dwelling bacteria that have historically been a major source of clinically important antibiotics.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Fungi are the source of penicillin, cephalosporins and griseofulvin, not this group of antibiotics.
  • Gram-negative bacteria is an incorrect source category; polymyxin B, colistin and bacitracin are sourced from bacteria (Bacillus species), not gram-negative organisms specifically.
  • Viruses are not used as a source for antibiotic production in this classification.
Know More
  • Polymyxin B, colistin, and bacitracin are examples of antibiotics sourced from bacteria (Bacillus species).
  • Griseofulvin is sourced from fungi.
  • This source-based classification is one of several ways antimicrobials are classified, alongside chemical nature, mechanism, and spectrum.
  • Streptomyces is a genus of Actinomycetes responsible for producing many antibiotics.

posts.post_content: Based on mechanism of action, fluoroquinolones are classified together with which action listed in the classification of antimicrobial agents?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Inhibit DNA gyrase

Fluoroquinolones are classified under agents that inhibit DNA gyrase.

Correct Option Explanation

DNA gyrase is essential for controlling supercoiling of bacterial DNA, and its inhibition disrupts DNA replication and transcription, producing a bactericidal effect.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Inhibiting cell wall synthesis is the mechanism of penicillin, cephalosporin, cycloserine, vancomycin and bacitracin, not fluoroquinolones.
  • Causing leakage from cell membrane describes the action of polypeptides and polyenes.
  • Inhibiting protein synthesis describes tetracyclines, chloramphenicol, erythromycin and clindamycin, a different mechanistic group.
Know More
  • Aminoglycosides act by causing misreading of the mRNA code and affecting permeability.
  • Sulfonamides, sulfones, PAS and trimethoprim interfere with intermediary metabolism.
  • Rifampin and metronidazole interfere with DNA function.
  • Fluoroquinolones show a bactericidal action that is rapid and concentration dependent.

posts.post_title: Who developed sulfa from the prodrug Prontos…
posts.post_content: Sulfa drugs were developed from the prodrug azo dye Prontosil by which scientist in 1935?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Gerhard Domagk

Gerhard Domagk developed sulfa from the prodrug Prontosil in 1935.

Correct Option Explanation

Prontosil was used to treat streptococcal infection in mice, and Domagk received the Nobel Prize for medicine in 1939 for this work.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin, a different antibiotic class, not sulfa drugs.
  • Paul Ehrlich developed arsenicals in the earlier dye and organometallic phase of chemotherapy, before Prontosil.
  • Selman Waksman discovered streptomycin in 1944, unrelated to the sulfa drug development.
Know More
  • Sulfa is classified as a non-antibiotic, referred to as an antibacterial.
  • Sulfonamides are synthetic drugs derived from sulfanilamide.
  • Sulfonamides are weak organic acids with a pKa ranging from 4.99 to 8.56.
  • Sulfacetamide is a neutral preparation used for ophthalmic purposes.

posts.post_content: Which of the following organisms shows good susceptibility to sulfonamides?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Streptococci

Streptococci show good susceptibility to sulfonamides.

Correct Option Explanation

Good susceptibility is also seen with Actinomycetes, Bacillus, Brucella, Listeria, Chlamydia, and Cryptosporidium.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Pseudomonas is listed as resistant to sulfonamides.
  • Mycobacteria are resistant to sulfonamides.
  • Mycoplasma is also listed among the organisms resistant to sulfonamides.
Know More
  • Staphylococcus and Enterococcus show only moderate susceptibility to sulfonamides.
  • Sulfonamides are broad spectrum and bacteriostatic, but become bactericidal at higher urine concentrations.
  • Resistant organisms include Mycoplasma, Rickettsia, Spirochetes and Pseudomonas.
  • Sulfonamides are active against Chlamydia, Toxoplasma and Coccidia as well as bacteria.

posts.post_title: Poorly absorbed sulfonamide used for enteric…
posts.post_content: Which sulfonamide is poorly absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, making it useful for treating enteric infections?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Sulfasalazine

Sulfasalazine is poorly absorbed from the GIT, making it useful in enteric infection.

Correct Option Explanation

Sulfasalazine is broken down to sulfapyridine and 5-amino salicylic acid in the colon, and is used to treat chronic colitis at 25 mg/kg TID for 2-4 weeks in dogs.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Sulfadiazine is a systemic/general-purpose sulfonamide, not classified as gut-acting.
  • Sulfamethoxazole is used as a potentiated sulfonamide in combination with trimethoprim, not as a gut-acting agent.
  • Sulfisoxazole is a highly soluble sulfonamide used for urinary tract infections, being rapidly absorbed and excreted through the kidney rather than remaining in the gut.
Know More
  • Other gut-acting sulfonamides include phthalylsulfathiazole, succinylsulfathiazole, and sulfaguanidine.
  • Triple sulfa combines sulfamerazine, sulfapyridine and sulfadiazine to act additively while reducing crystalluria risk.
  • Silver sulfadiazine and mafenide are topical sulfonamides used for burn wounds.
  • Sulfacetamide is used for ophthalmic purposes as a neutral preparation.

posts.post_content: Sulfonamide-induced crystalluria and renal colic primarily result from deposition of which metabolic form of the drug in renal tubules?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Acetylated derivatives

Acetylated derivatives of sulfa deposit in renal tubules, pelvis and ureter, causing crystalluria.

Correct Option Explanation

This deposition causes renal colic, hematuria, obstruction of the renal tubule and increased BUN level, especially under acidic urine and low water intake.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Aromatic hydroxylation and glucuronide conjugation actually make the drug more water soluble, reducing crystalluria risk rather than causing it.
  • Glucuronide conjugates similarly increase water solubility and are not the cause of crystal deposition.
  • The unmetabolized parent drug is not specifically implicated; it is the acetylated metabolite that is less soluble and deposits in tubules.
Know More
  • Alkalinisation of urine with sodium bicarbonate helps prevent crystalluria.
  • Incidence of crystalluria is less with sulfisoxazole.
  • Triple sulfa combinations reduce crystalluria risk because each component is excreted individually at lower concentration.
  • Treatment with sulfonamides should not exceed seven days.

posts.post_title: Ratio of sulfadoxine combined with trimethop…
posts.post_content: Potentiated sulfonamide preparations combine sulfadoxine with trimethoprim in what ratio?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 5:1

Sulfadoxine is combined with trimethoprim in a 5:1 ratio.

Correct Option Explanation

This potentiated combination exploits sequential blockade of the folate synthesis pathway, making the combination bactericidal even though each drug alone is bacteriostatic.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • A 1:1 ratio is not the combination ratio used for potentiated sulfonamides in this text.
  • A 10:1 ratio is not the described ratio for sulfadoxine-trimethoprim combination.
  • A 1:5 ratio reverses the actual proportion; trimethoprim is the minor component at 1 part to sulfa's 5 parts.
Know More
  • Sulfadiazine is also used in potentiated combination with trimethoprim.
  • Triple sulfa (sulfamerazine + sulfapyridine + sulfadiazine) act additively but are excreted individually to reduce adverse effects.
  • Diaminopyrimidines like trimethoprim and ormethoprim act synergistically with sulfonamides.
  • Sulfonamides plus chlortetracycline act as a growth promoter and help prevent clostridial enterotoxemia.

posts.post_content: According to the principles of sulphonamide therapy, treatment should generally not exceed how many days?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Seven days

Sulfonamide treatment should not exceed seven days.

Correct Option Explanation

This principle limits the risk of toxicity such as crystalluria while ensuring the therapy is started early, since sulfonamides are ineffective in chronic cases.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Three days is too short; while a favorable response is expected within four to five days, treatment duration itself extends to seven days if needed.
  • Five days is the point by which a favorable response should be seen, not the maximum treatment duration.
  • Fourteen days exceeds the maximum recommended duration and increases the risk of toxicity.
Know More
  • If no favourable response is seen within four to five days, therapy should be discontinued.
  • Treatment should continue 48 hours after remission in some cases to prevent recurrence.
  • Sulfonamides should be started at the early stage of infection since they are ineffective in chronic cases.
  • Adequate drinking water should be administered during therapy to prevent crystalluria.

posts.post_content: Which topical sulfonamide is used for burn wounds and is effective against Pseudomonas?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Silver sulfadiazine

Silver sulfadiazine (along with mafenide) is used topically for burn wounds and is effective against Pseudomonas.

Correct Option Explanation

These topical agents prevent infection in burn wounds specifically because of their activity against Pseudomonas, a common burn-wound pathogen.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Sulfacetamide is used for ophthalmic purposes, not burn wounds.
  • Sulfaguanidine is a gut-acting sulfonamide poorly absorbed from the GIT, used for enteric infections.
  • Sulfisoxazole is a highly soluble sulfonamide used for urinary tract infections due to rapid renal excretion.
Know More
  • Mafenide is the other topical sulfonamide used alongside silver sulfadiazine for burn wounds.
  • Sulfacetamide is a neutral preparation suitable for ophthalmic use.
  • Highly soluble sulfonamides for UTI include sulfisoxazole and sulfasomidine.
  • Sulfonamides are also used clinically for colibacillosis, pasteurellosis and footrot.

posts.post_title: Sulfa drug used for dermatitis herpetiformis…
posts.post_content: Which sulfa-related compound, chemically known as diaminophenyl sulphone, is used to treat dermatitis herpetiformis in dogs and leprosy in humans?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Dapsone

Dapsone, a diaminophenyl sulphone, is used for dermatitis herpetiformis in dogs and leprosy in humans.

Correct Option Explanation

Dapsone belongs to the broader sulfa-related class but has a specific clinical niche distinct from typical antibacterial sulfonamides.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Sulfadiazine is a systemic/general-purpose sulfonamide used for common bacterial infections, not dermatitis herpetiformis.
  • Sulfaguanidine is a gut-acting sulfonamide used for enteric infections.
  • Sulfamethoxazole is used in potentiated combination with trimethoprim for systemic infections.
Know More
  • Sulfonamides in poultry are used to prevent or treat coccidiosis, infectious coryza, pullorum disease and fowl typhoid.
  • Colibacillosis and pasteurellosis are among the clinical uses of general-purpose sulfonamides.
  • PABA antagonizes sulfonamides by competing for the same enzymatic pathway.
  • Sulfonamides can cause decreased egg production and thin-shelled eggs in poultry.

posts.post_content: Trimethoprim exerts its antibacterial action by inhibiting which enzyme?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR)

Trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR).

Correct Option Explanation

This causes a sequential blockade of the folate pathway when combined with a sulfonamide, and trimethoprim is roughly 50,000 times more selective for bacterial DHFR than mammalian DHFR.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • DNA gyrase is the target of fluoroquinolones, not trimethoprim.
  • Peptidyl transferase is inhibited by chloramphenicol and lincosamides, part of protein synthesis inhibition.
  • Beta-lactamase is an enzyme produced by resistant bacteria, and is the target of beta-lactamase inhibitors like clavulanic acid, not trimethoprim's mechanism.
Know More
  • Trimethoprim alone is bacteriostatic; combined with sulfa it becomes bactericidal.
  • Co-trimoxazole is the fixed-dose combination of sulfamethoxazole plus trimethoprim.
  • Trimethoprim is poorly soluble in water and is a weak organic base with pKa 7.6.
  • It accumulates in acidic urine, milk and ruminal fluid.

posts.post_title: Trimethoprim side effect specific to Doberma…
posts.post_content: Which trimethoprim-associated adverse effect has been specifically reported in Doberman dogs?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Transient arthritis

Transient arthritis has been specifically reported in Dobermans following trimethoprim use.

Correct Option Explanation

This breed-specific adverse reaction is one among several documented trimethoprim side effects that also include folate deficiency and ocular effects.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Keratoconjunctivitis from reduced lacrimal secretion is a general trimethoprim side effect, not specifically linked to Dobermans.
  • Idiosyncratic thrombocytopenia is a separate adverse reaction not specifically tied to the Doberman breed in this text.
  • Salivation is specifically noted with uncoated oral tablets in cats, not Dobermans.
Know More
  • Folate deficiency can cause megaloblastic anemia, treatable with folinic acid administration.
  • Cats may show salivation after uncoated oral tablets.
  • A withdrawal period of about three days is generally needed after trimethoprim use.
  • Trimethoprim readily absorbs after oral administration except in ruminants, where it undergoes microbial degradation.

posts.post_content: What percentage of trimethoprim is bound to plasma proteins?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 30-60%

Trimethoprim is 30% to 60% protein bound.

Correct Option Explanation

It is also widely distributed in tissues including the prostate, and is partly metabolized in the liver before excretion via glomerular filtration and tubular secretion.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 10-20% is lower than the stated binding range for trimethoprim.
  • 70-90% overstates the binding range; this level is closer to some other antimicrobials like clindamycin.
  • Above 95% is far higher than trimethoprim's actual reported protein binding.
Know More
  • Trimethoprim is used for UTI, enteric infection, salmonella and brucellosis.

  • Direct destruction of the shell gland is not the mechanism described for DDT-induced egg shell thinning in this text.

Know More
  • DDT increases intracellular sodium and calcium of excitable cells via two mechanisms.
  • DDT is metabolized to DDD and DDE, with DDE permanently stored in adipose tissue.

posts.post_content: Pyrethroids such as permethrin and cypermethrin cause arthropod paralysis by which mechanism, and should not be used in which species?

_aimcq_options.text: Prolonging sodium channel opening; should not be used in cats
Blocking chloride channels; should not be used in dogs
Inhibiting acetylcholinesterase; should not be used in horses
Activating octopamine receptors; should not be used in cattle

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Prolonging sodium channel opening; should not be used in cats

Pyrethroids act by prolonging the opening of sodium channels, causing arthropod paralysis, and should not be used in cats.

Correct Option Explanation

These alkaloids of pyrethrum are generally safe in other species but can cause local irritation, hypersalivation and vomiting, and specifically pose toxicity risks in cats.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Blocking chloride channels; should not be used in dogs misattributes both the mechanism (chloride channel blocking describes lindane, not pyrethroids) and the species restriction.
  • Inhibiting acetylcholinesterase; should not be used in horses misattributes the mechanism (this describes OPCs) and the species restriction for pyrethroids.
  • Activating octopamine receptors; should not be used in cattle misattributes the mechanism (this describes amitraz) and the species restriction for pyrethroids.
Know More
  • Examples of pyrethroids include allethrin, cypermethrin, fenvalerate, and permethrin.
  • They are alkaloids derived from pyrethrum.
  • Adverse effects can include local irritation, hypersalivation and vomiting.
  • Cats' specific sensitivity relates to their limited ability to metabolize these compounds via glucuronidation.

posts.post_content: According to standard definitions, a disinfectant is applied to inanimate objects, while an antiseptic is characteristically applied to what?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Living tissue

An antiseptic is applied to living tissue to prevent or arrest microbial growth.

Correct Option Explanation

In contrast, a disinfectant refers to substances applied to inanimate objects to destroy disease-causing microorganisms.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Air only is not the defining application site for antiseptics; some disinfection methods do address air/room fumigation, but that is not the antiseptic definition.
  • Water supplies only describes one specific disinfectant application (e.g., chlorination), not the general antiseptic definition.
  • Soil is not the characteristic application site described for antiseptics in this text.
Know More
  • A high-level disinfectant is active against bacterial endospores.
  • An intermediate-level disinfectant inactivates tubercle bacilli but not spores.
  • A low-level disinfectant rapidly kills vegetative bacteria and fungi but not tubercle bacilli or spores.
  • Most disinfectants kill bacteria rapidly (within minutes), while antibiotics may only be bacteriostatic or act after several hours.

posts.post_content: Chlorine, a strong oxidizing agent used as a disinfectant, exerts its antimicrobial effect primarily by which mechanism?

Chlorine acts by oxidation of peptide links and denaturation of protein.

Its accumulation inhibits essential enzyme systems, but chlorine is inactivated in the presence of organic matter, limiting its effectiveness in dirty conditions.

posts.post_content: Povidone-iodine, an iodophor complexing iodine with polyvinylpyrrolidone, offers which advantage over simple tincture iodine?

Converts iodine into a sporicidal-only agent

posts.post_content: Cationic detergents such as quaternary ammonium compounds are primarily used for disinfecting floors, walls and equipment surfaces, and are active in which type of medium?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Alkaline medium

Cationic detergents are active in alkaline medium.

Correct Option Explanation

They bind irreversibly to phospholipids and proteins of the cytoplasmic membrane, impairing permeability and causing a bactericidal effect against both gram-positive (at higher concentration) and gram-negative bacteria.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Mild acid solution is the medium in which anionic detergents (like soaps) are active, not cationic detergents.

posts.post_content: Chlorhexidine hydrochloride, a potent bactericidal agent active against both gram-positive and gram-negative organisms, is ineffective against which group of pathogens?

  • Only aerobic bacteria is not the described spectrum limitation; the actual limitation is against fungi, virus and spores, not a specific bacterial oxygen requirement.

  • Chlorhexidine is incompatible with soap and anionic detergents.
